question: Does regular low-dose aspirin use reduce the long-term risk of colorectal cancer?
answer_text: Yes. In a long-term follow-up of randomized trials, regular low-dose aspirin was associated with a reduced incidence of colorectal cancer, with the benefit emerging after about ten years of follow-up [1]. A pooled cohort analysis reported a similar direction of effect, though absolute risk reduction was modest [2].
rationale: Both cited passages report a reduction in colorectal cancer incidence with sustained low-dose aspirin use.

question: Is vitamin D supplementation effective for preventing acute respiratory tract infections in the general population?
answer_text: The evidence is mixed. A meta-analysis of randomized trials found a small overall protective effect that was concentrated in participants with baseline deficiency, and not clearly present otherwise [1]. Effect sizes varied with dosing schedule [1].
rationale: The cited meta-analysis reports a subgroup-dependent effect rather than a consistent general-population benefit, which maps to maybe.

contexts.title: Vitamin D supplementation to prevent acute respiratory infections: systematic review and meta-analysis
contexts.text: Vitamin D supplementation reduced the risk of acute respiratory tract infection overall, but the protective effect was strongest among participants with baseline 25-hydroxyvitamin D below 25 nmol per litre and was attenuated in those who were replete. Daily or weekly dosing appeared more effective than bolus dosing.
contexts.support: the protective effect was strongest among participants with baseline 25-hydroxyvitamin D below 25 nmol per litre and was attenuated in those who were replete

contexts.title: Vitamin D status and respiratory outcomes in a cohort
contexts.text: Lower serum vitamin D was associated with more frequent respiratory infections in an observational cohort, but causality could not be established.

contexts.title: Vitamin D and asthma exacerbations
contexts.text: Vitamin D reduced the rate of asthma exacerbations requiring systemic corticosteroids in a subgroup analysis.

contexts.title: Micronutrients and immune function
contexts.text: Several micronutrients including vitamin D contribute to immune function, though supplementation effects in replete individuals are uncertain.

question: Does intermittent fasting improve long-term cardiovascular mortality compared with continuous calorie restriction?
rationale: The retrieved passages address short-term weight and metabolic markers, not long-term cardiovascular mortality, so the system abstains rather than guess.

contexts.title: Intermittent fasting and metabolic markers: a randomized trial
contexts.text: Intermittent fasting produced weight loss and improved insulin sensitivity over 12 weeks, comparable to continuous calorie restriction. Cardiovascular events were not assessed.

contexts.title: Time-restricted eating and body weight
contexts.text: Time-restricted eating reduced body weight modestly over 12 weeks without a control-group difference in lean mass.

contexts.title: Caloric restriction and longevity in animal models
contexts.text: Caloric restriction extends lifespan in several animal models; translation to human cardiovascular mortality remains unproven.

contexts.title: Dietary patterns and cardiovascular risk factors
